prompt:

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?

   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?

   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Vertex fits several Rule Breaker traits: it is the dominant innovator in cystic fibrosis, has a sustainable advantage through patents to 2037-2039, strong management and a share price up about 170% over five years. It falls short on being a top dog in a big emerging industry and on consumer brand recognition, and analysts rate it Buy rather than call it overvalued.
summaries.buffett: Vertex has an exceptionally durable moat in cystic fibrosis, high returns on capital (ROIC around 29%), no debt before the Crinetics deal and an 86% gross margin. The drawbacks for Buffett are that biotech pipelines are hard to forecast, about 96% of revenue comes from one disease area, and a P/E near 29 offers little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the lollapalooza of CF know-how, patents and lifelong patient use that makes Vertex nearly a monopoly. He would be wary of single-franchise concentration, drug-pricing politics and paying about 29 times earnings for a business whose next growth engines are still unproven.
summaries.lynch: Vertex is a stalwart-to-fast-grower with a simple story: own cystic fibrosis and use the cash to build new franchises in pain, kidney disease and diabetes. With revenue growing about 10% and a P/E near 29, its PEG is well above 1, and it is widely covered on Wall Street, so it is not a classic Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: Vertex scores well on Fisher's points: large R&D ($3.9B in 2025) that produced Casgevy, Alyftrek and Journavx, high margins, a strong research culture and long-term management. Its sales growth beyond CF depends on new launches that have started slowly, which is the main Fisher-style question.
summaries.graham: Vertex fails most of Graham's defensive criteria: it pays no dividend, posted net losses in 2016 and 2024, and trades at about 29 times earnings and roughly 6 times book value. Its strong balance sheet is the main point in its favour.
summaries.thiel: Vertex is a near-textbook Thiel monopoly in cystic fibrosis: proprietary CFTR science far better than any alternative, a small market it dominated first, and durable patents. Whether it can recreate that monopoly in pain, kidney disease and type 1 diabetes is the open question.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would like Vertex's profitability (38% trailing operating margin), roughly 30% free-cash-flow margin and disciplined buybacks, but revenue growth around 10% and a forward P/E near 28 make it a fair-priced compounder rather than a mispriced high-growth story.
summaries.druckenmiller: Near-term catalysts (povetacicept decision November 30, 2026, Q3 results, Crinetics' Palsonify launch) and a share price beating the market give some momentum, but earnings estimates have been flat to slightly down and growth is steady rather than accelerating, so Druckenmiller-style conviction would be moderate.
summaries.smith: Vertex matches Terry Smith's 'good company' test with high returns on capital, high gross margins, strong cash conversion and low reliance on debt. A ~3% free-cash-flow yield means investors are not getting it cheaply, and Smith would watch capital allocation after the $10B Crinetics purchase.
summaries.greenblatt: Return on capital is high, but the earnings yield is low: trailing operating income of about $4.8B against an enterprise value near $115B gives roughly 4%, so Vertex would not rank highly on the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: Vertex fits Akre's stool well on business quality (a CF near-monopoly with high returns) and reasonably on management, with a CEO who has delivered three new approvals. The reinvestment leg relies on R&D and acquisitions such as Crinetics, whose returns are less certain than its CF reinvestment has been.
summaries.pabrai: Vertex is not a Dhandho bet: it is a well-known, fully priced quality company rather than a distressed business with heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose-much odds, although its no-debt balance sheet before the Crinetics deal limited the downside.
summaries.wood: Vertex touches ARK's themes through CRISPR gene editing (Casgevy) and stem-cell-derived islet therapy (zimislecel), but its revenue is dominated by small-molecule CF drugs, and cell and gene therapy costs are not yet falling enough to unlock mass demand.
summaries.ackman: Vertex meets many of Ackman's criteria: simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating, dominant in its niche with high barriers to entry and a strong balance sheet. Its drug-pricing and pipeline exposure and a full valuation would make him seek a catalyst or a lower price.
summaries.sleep: Vertex shows some scale-economics thinking (CF profits funding R&D that keeps extending the franchise), but it does not pass scale savings to customers through lower prices as Nomad's favourites such as Costco did; its model rests on premium pricing.
summaries.valentine: Vertex solves huge, painful problems (fatal genetic disease, opioid-free pain, type 1 diabetes) with hard-to-copy technology, the kind of market Valentine prized, though today it is a large established company rather than an early-stage venture.
summaries.nash: Vertex passes many of Nash's quality tests: more cash than debt at mid-2026, about 38% trailing operating margin, low short interest, high institutional ownership and a strong moat, and it scores about 115 of 130 on his 13 categories. It fails on revenue growth that is only around 10%, two small EPS misses in the last four quarters, operating margins lower than five years ago, and a DCF value well below today's $499.74 price.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $499.74 on October 16, 2026, up about 22.5% over 52 weeks versus about a 16% total return for the S&P 500 (SPY), and up about 14% in the month after Q2 results.

g4.evidence: CEO Reshma Kewalramani has delivered three new approvals since 2020, and Vertex partners with CRISPR Therapeutics on Casgevy; institutions own about 97% of the shares.

g6.evidence: Analysts are mostly bullish (20 Strong Buy, 6 Buy, 5 Hold, 1 Strong Sell; average target $571.46), not calling the stock overvalued.

simple.evidence: The CF franchise is easy to understand (lifelong daily pills with no rival), but judging pipeline bets in gene editing, kidney disease and cell therapy needs specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $6,205.7M in 2020 to $12,001.3M in 2025, and net income was positive in every year except 2024, when the Alpine acquired-IPR&D charge caused a loss.

integrity.evidence: Vertex reports clearly, buys back stock and has no accounting controversies, but executive pay relies heavily on stock-based compensation ($650M-$700M expected in 2026).

b6.evidence: Vertex sticks to its strategy of serious diseases with validated biology, but it has made large acquisitions (Alpine for about $4.9B in 2024, Crinetics for about $10B in 2026).

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 28.8% (StockAnalysis) and Vertex had no borrowings at June 30, 2026.

fcf.evidence: Trailing-twelve-month operating cash flow was $4,292.9M and free cash flow about $3,796M, roughly 86% of TTM GAAP net income of about $4,405M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings reached $15,691.2M at June 30, 2026, and market value rose from roughly $60B at the end of 2020 to about $127B, more than the earnings retained.

safety.evidence: At $499.74 the stock trades at about 29 times trailing GAAP earnings and a Nash-style DCF gives roughly $200-$300 per share, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E near 28 and ~3% FCF yield are full for ~10% revenue growth, though arguably fair for a near-monopoly with 86% gross margins and a large pipeline.

mu5.evidence: CF exclusivity to 2037-2039 limits failure modes, but heavy CF concentration, US drug-pricing policy and the Royalty Pharma Alyftrek royalty dispute are real ways the thesis could weaken.

reinvest.evidence: Vertex reinvests heavily ($3.9B R&D in 2025, $10B for Crinetics), and its CF reinvestment earned very high returns, but returns on newer bets such as Casgevy and Journavx are not yet proven.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: dominate cystic fibrosis, then use the cash to build franchises in pain, kidney disease, type 1 diabetes and endocrinology.

ly3.evidence: The P/E is about 29 versus expected EPS growth of about 10%, giving a PEG near 2.8.

runway.evidence: Beyond CF, suzetrigine in diabetic neuropathy (Phase 3), povetacicept (PDUFA November 30, 2026), zimislecel and Palsonify give multiple multi-billion-dollar opportunities.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 263.4M in 2020 to 255.2M in Q2 2026 through buybacks ($2,017.4M in 2025), but insider ownership is only about 0.2% and there is no sign of open-market insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Vertex is a $127B S&P 500 company covered by more than 30 analysts.

fi2.evidence: As Trikafta matures, Vertex launched Alyftrek, Casgevy and Journavx and acquired Palsonify, with povetacicept and zimislecel next.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced the full CF modulator series, the first CRISPR therapy (Casgevy, 2023) and the first new pain class in about 20 years (Journavx, 2025).

fi4.evidence: Vertex sells superbly in CF, converting patients quickly to Alyftrek ($573.6M in Q2 2026), but Casgevy ($115.8M in 2025) and Journavx ($59.6M) launches have been slow.

longterm.evidence: It keeps spending about a third of revenue on R&D and funds long-horizon programs like stem-cell islets for type 1 diabetes.

gr1.evidence: Vertex had $12,001.3M of revenue in 2025 and a market value around $127B.

ni10.evidence: Vertex reported a GAAP net loss of $535.6M in 2024 (Alpine IPR&D charge) and also lost money in 2016.

gr4.evidence: Vertex has never paid a dividend; it returns cash through buybacks.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from a loss in 2015 to $15.32 in 2025, far more than a one-third increase.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 29 times trailing GAAP EPS of about $17.17, well above 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 29 times price-to-book of about 6.3 gives roughly 180, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: In CF Vertex's modulators are the only drugs that correct the underlying protein defect, a step-change no rival has matched.

timing.evidence: Gene editing, non-opioid pain and stem-cell therapies are now reaching approval (Casgevy 2023, Journavx 2025), and Vertex has the cash to commercialise them.

th3.evidence: Vertex started with a near-total share of the small CF market and is expanding into sickle cell, pain, kidney disease and endocrinology.

team.evidence: Kewalramani, a physician-scientist, has led Vertex since 2020, delivering three approvals while revenue nearly doubled from $6,205.7M (2020) to $12,001.3M (2025), backed by a deep scientific bench.

th5.evidence: Vertex has a global commercial footprint and close ties to CF care centers, and it is building specialty sales forces for pain, nephrology and endocrinology.

durable.evidence: CF exclusivity runs to 2037-2039 and next-generation drugs extend it, but long-term durability depends on new franchises and on genetic medicines that could one day cure CF.

th7.evidence: Vertex saw early that CFTR could be corrected with small molecules, a bet others did not pursue, but its newer areas are crowded (IgAN has Otsuka, Vera and Novartis).

trend.evidence: It benefits from the rise of genetic medicine and precision therapies, but it is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift like AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth is steady at about 10%, and Zacks noted downward estimate revisions after Q2 2026, when adjusted EPS of $4.73 slightly missed.

dr2.evidence: Possible povetacicept approval (PDUFA November 30, 2026), the Palsonify launch and Phase 3 progress for suzetrigine and zimislecel could make the business look better by 2028, though some of this is expected.

dr4.evidence: Demand for rare-disease medicines barely depends on the economy or interest rates, but US drug-pricing policy (MFN, GUARD model) is a headwind.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the povetacicept FDA decision (November 30, 2026), inaxaplin interim data (early 2027), Q3 results around November 2, 2026 and Palsonify sales.

dr7.evidence: CF dominance supports conviction, but CF concentration and pipeline binary risk argue against an outsized position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 86.2% in 2025 ($12,001.3M revenue, $1,651.3M cost of sales).

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $3.8B gives roughly a 3.0% yield on a ~$127B market cap, fair but not cheap for ~10% growth.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $4,777M against an enterprise value near $115B is an earnings yield of only about 4%.

pa2.evidence: Vertex is not in a setback; revenue grew 12% in Q2 2026 and guidance was raised.

pa4.evidence: With CF exclusivity into the late 2030s, about $12B+ of annual revenue and very low leverage, permanent loss of capital looks unlikely even if pipeline bets fail, though valuation risk remains.

wo1.evidence: Vertex is a leader in gene editing (first approved CRISPR therapy, Casgevy), part of ARK's multiomic theme, but most revenue comes from conventional small-molecule drugs.

wo2.evidence: Casgevy remains a costly, complex one-time therapy (64 patients infused in 2025), and costs are not yet falling enough to unlock mass demand.

wo3.evidence: It combines small-molecule drug discovery, CRISPR gene editing, stem-cell-derived cell therapy and biologics (povetacicept).

wo4.evidence: Success in type 1 diabetes, diabetic neuropathy pain and kidney disease could multiply its addressable market, but within five years that depends on uncertain trials.

ac3.evidence: As a rare-disease drug maker with 86% gross margins and no debt at mid-2026, Vertex is largely insulated from commodity prices and interest rates.

ns1.evidence: Vertex's model relies on high prices; it cited higher CF net prices in 2025 rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: If povetacicept, zimislecel and suzetrigine succeed Vertex will be far more diversified than today, but that outcome is not assured.

va2.evidence: Its medicines tackle fatal or debilitating diseases such as cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, severe pain without addiction risk and type 1 diabetes.

tn1.evidence: Vertex was built for precision and genetic medicine, a lasting trend, but not one of Nash's preferred infrastructure trends such as AI or energy.

tn2.evidence: The market still sees Vertex as a CF company while it builds franchises in pain, kidney disease, diabetes and endocrinology, though that ambition is widely discussed.

tn3.evidence: It is a $127B US company founded in 1989, outside small caps, China, commodities, airlines and seasonal businesses.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year since 2020, it is profitable (2025 net income $3,953.2M), and at June 30, 2026 it had $13.6B of cash and investments and no borrowings.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in Q1 2025 (~$778M), Q2 2025 (~$927M), H2 2025 (~$1,488M), Q1 2026 (~$1,295M) and Q2 2026 (~$1,013M), with no borrowings through June 30, 2026.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 8.9% in 2025 and 10.2% in the first half of 2026, with 2026 guidance implying about 9.6%; it is right around the 10% bar.

tn7.evidence: First-half 2026 revenue growth of 10.2% plus a trailing FCF margin of about 30% gives roughly 40, but 2025's 8.9% growth plus 26.6% FCF margin was only about 35.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 8.9% while total costs and expenses fell from $11,253.0M to $7,828.0M; in H1 2026 revenue rose 10.2% while costs fell slightly.

tn9.evidence: It passes on size, cash, short interest (~1.8%), operating margin (~38%) and age, but non-GAAP EPS slightly missed consensus in Q4 2025 ($5.03 vs $5.05) and Q2 2026 ($4.73 vs $4.74), two misses in four quarters.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential legal threat, but US drug-pricing policy (CMS GUARD proposal, Part D redesign) and the Royalty Pharma arbitration over the Alyftrek royalty (8% vs 4%) are notable risks.

tn11.evidence: Vertex provides medicines that correct the cause of cystic fibrosis, helping patients breathe and live longer, and charges insurers per-patient prices for lifelong daily therapy; no competitor offers an equivalent.

tn13.evidence: Score about 115/130: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 5, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 10, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 10, secular trend 5, culture and mission 10, talent 10.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year, but operating margin fell from 46.0% (2020) to 34.8% (2025) and free cash flow was negative in 2024 (about -$790M) because of the Alpine purchase.

tn15.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Vertex had no borrowings, assets excluding goodwill of $26,335.3M vs liabilities of $7,175.4M (3.7x), a current ratio of 3.19 and liabilities of 0.35x equity.

tn18.evidence: Kewalramani has executed well since 2020 (revenue nearly doubled, three approvals), but she has been CEO for about six years, is not a founder and has no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Over the last six quarters non-GAAP EPS beat consensus four times by Marketbeat's count but missed slightly in Q4 2025 and Q2 2026, while revenue usually beat.

tn21.evidence: No accounting issues, auditor change or co-CEOs, but operating margins are lower than in 2020 and the company has made two large acquisitions (Alpine, Crinetics) in three years.

tn22.evidence: Vertex has $12B of revenue, strong profits and buys back shares rather than issuing them.

tn24.evidence: Nash's DCF at 12% gives roughly $200-$300 per share, so the $499.74 price implies faster growth or higher margins than the ~10% growth and ~27-30% FCF margin it is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages (10.4% revenue growth, 17.8% FCF margin, depressed by 2024), 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and $13.6B of cash, value is about $195 per share, and even at a 30% FCF margin about $290, below $499.74.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E near 28 against EPS growth of about 10% gives a PEG near 2.8, above 1 and above many large-pharma peers.
